en: <1>Why is the storefront part of what you get?</1>
<1>Where does this show up in your daily life?</1>
<1>Do you really choose on your own?</1>
<1>What does the platform promise without saying it?</1>
<1>What must the platform guarantee?</1>
<1>And if the platform changes the rules of the game?</1>
<1>Who decides what you see in an online store or on a social network?</1>

ANDRADE, Victor L. P. Quem decide o que você vê numa loja virtual ou numa rede social?. <1>Lex Plataformae</1>, version 0.11, 10/11/2026. Available at https://lexplataformae.com.br/plataformas/infraestrutura-e-intermediacao/
You look for a product in an online store, compare prices, check the reviews and pick the seller who seems most reliable. Or you open a social network and see what…
You turn on the delivery or ride app, accept requests and get paid per task. The contract says you are an independent partner and can log on and off whenever you want.

But the app is what hands out the requests, gives the ratings, decides who gets priority and applies the penalties. And one day the requests dry up, your earnings drop or your account is restricted, and you do not know what changed or why.
What does the app supply to those who work on it?
It looks like the app only pays per ride, delivery or task. But what it really supplies is the very place where your work becomes possible.

Without it you have no access to customers, you do not know how much you can earn and you do not stay in the queue for requests. That is why what you use is not a static thing or a service performed for you from the outside, but a work environment the app governs.
Your income is not earned somewhere else and simply routed through the app. It depends on the way the app was built and on how it changes.
In this family, the central utility is not reduced to the final payment per ride, delivery or completed task.<1>p. 765</1>
The object enjoyed, here, is neither a static good nor a simple service externally provided to the worker.<1>p. 765</1>
It is a governed productive environment, without which everyday economic activity does not become viable on the terms in which the platform itself promised and structured it.<1>p. 765</1>
Why doesn't a contract that talks about autonomy settle the matter?
The terms of use of the big delivery and ride apps repeat that you are independent, that the company only connects you with customers and that there is no boss and no exclusivity.

Yet those same terms include ratings, review of complaints, acceptance metrics, temporary ride restrictions and account deactivation. Independence stays on paper, while control lives in day-to-day operations.
So it is not enough to know whether you can turn the app on and off. What matters is that everything you need to work is offered, adjusted and changed by a system you do not control.

The instruments used by iFood, 99Food, Uber and 99 insist, with variations in language, on characterizing the partners as independent, on presenting the platform as an environment of technological intermediation and on ruling out a hierarchical bond or mandatory exclusivity.<1>p. 765</1>

It is a matter of recognizing that the functional utility indispensable to carrying out the economic activity is offered, modulated and reconfigured by a private architecture that the subject does not control.<1>p. 766</1>
Is this just a labor law issue?
It does not have to be. Here the question is not whether there is an employment relationship, or whether the whole relationship should become an employment contract.

The question is about what the app supplies and how it supplies it. This view does not turn everything into a labor case, but it also does not accept that a contract talking about autonomy closes the matter.
The focus, for the purposes of this typology, is on the regime of supply.<1>p. 766</1>
This application does not dissolve the subtype into undifferentiated labor law, but neither does it let itself be neutralized by contractual self-descriptions of formal autonomy.<1>p. 768</1>

<1>Semiotic vulnerability.</1> It is the disadvantage of someone who has to rely on signs that someone else controls. Here it is sharper, because you depend on the app not only to get requests but also to understand your position, your risk and your earnings.

Metrics, incentive messages, quality alerts, promotions and performance notifications work like a language that governs your behavior. And the one who has to decode that language, without being able to check what lies behind it, is you.
This is semiotic vulnerability associated with productive dependence.<1>p. 766</1>

It is a semiotic regime that organizes the subject's economic experience and shifts onto them the costs of interpreting an environment whose material functioning they cannot audit on their own.<1>p. 766</1>
<1>When the way requests are handed out changes without explanation.</1> Rides or deliveries become scarce, and you do not know whether it was demand, your rating or a new rule.
<1>When the pay calculation changes.</1> The same work starts earning less, and the parameters that would explain the difference stay hidden.
<1>When a restriction or a block comes.</1> The account is limited or deactivated, and you cannot link the penalty to a cause you can check.
<1>When the account stays active but is worth less.</1> The program name and the look of the partnership stay the same, but what justified your being there has been hollowed out.
All of this weighs more than a contractual nuisance, because it affects your income, how predictable your livelihood is and your chance to keep working.

Opacity about the distribution of opportunities, prioritization criteria, variable pay parameters, the effects of ratings and the causes of restrictions falls, in this context, not merely on abstract contractual comfort, but on the very material living conditions of people who depend on this environment to work.<1>p. 767</1>
Does an active account prove nothing changed?
It does not. The right question is not whether your account is still on.
The question is whether your place in the app is still worth what it was worth when it supported your expectation of earning and of staying there.
Showing that your earnings dropped or that the account was blocked once is not enough. The loss has to be connected to the way the app governs the work.
The history of requests.
The changes in pay.
The app's messages and performance alerts.
The criteria that were disclosed and those that were left out.
The records of restrictions and the ratings you received.
Before-and-after comparisons of the change.
Keep whatever you can while it is still accessible, such as screenshots, earnings statements and dates.
<1>Thinking lower earnings are just a risk of the job.</1> The drop may come from a rule change the app made without explanation.
<1>Looking only at the final penalty.</1> The block is usually the end of a story of targets, incentives and threats, and that story counts too.
<1>Thinking the lack of clarity is just how technology is.</1> Hiding metrics and criteria is not inevitable, and it is precisely part of the problem.
The second is to treat the final sanction as an isolated event, without reconstructing the regime of conduct, incentive and threat that preceded it.<1>p. 768</1>
The third is to accept the lack of transparency about metrics and criteria as an inevitable consequence of technology, when precisely this opacity is part of the central legal problem.<1>p. 768</1>
No one can demand that the app open up its entire system, and the judge does not become the platform's manager. But the changes that affect your work have to be checkable.
This applies to new rules, changes to the calculation, to priority and to metrics, and to penalties with real effects. Generic explanations about efficiency, security or the algorithm are not enough.
Without that minimum, the app holds two powers at once. The power to organize your work and the power to hide the facts you would need to challenge it.

Relevant rule changes, changes in calculation, reconfigurations of priority, redefinitions of metrics or sanctions with material impact cannot be shielded by a generic discourse of efficiency, security or algorithmic optimization. They must be made minimally verifiable.<1>p. 767</1>
This does not mean opening the system entirely, nor turning the Judiciary into the platform's technical administrator.<1>p. 767</1>
Without this minimum, the platform simultaneously concentrates the power to organize economic activity and the power to make opaque the facts needed to challenge it.<1>p. 767</1>

When the change hollows out your place in the app, it may be possible to ask for the records to be preserved and disclosed. It may also be possible to ask for restrictions to be explained in a way that can be checked and for the penalty criteria to be reviewed. And you may be able to ask for clarity on how requests are handed out and for what was degraded to be restored.
In the most serious cases, when targets, penalties and changes form a stable plan to make you accept losses and behave the way the app wants, the very purpose of the design may come into question.
Do you depend on the app for income, and not just for an occasional side gig?
Did the requests, the pay, the metrics or the rules change without a clear explanation?
Were you restricted, blocked or stripped of priority without a cause you can check?
Are you unable to reconstruct what happened without the app's records?
Enjoyment, therefore, is the productive enjoyment of a governed environment. The platform worker consumes the very infrastructure that makes them economically operative.<1>p. 766</1>
